activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
story:
Ryder's trumpet squealed on the high G for the ninth time in a row, and the sound bounced off the music room's steel shelves like a trapped bird. Auditions for the spring ensemble were on Friday, and it was already Tuesday. Three days to get through the whole piece without a train wreck. He tipped the horn back, wiped his mouth, and started again from measure one.

"Again?" Emile looked up from the timpani in the corner, where he'd been pretending to practice while actually watching. "You've played that song like a million times since September."

"That's the point," Ryder said. "I'm going to wear it smooth." But by measure sixteen, the same crack in the same place, like a loose board in a floor he kept stepping on. His lips buzzed and ached. The room smelled of valve oil and old radiator dust, and the radiators had just clanked on with a sound like a monsoon hitting a tin roof, hard and sudden and everywhere at once.

Lisa came in for her cello lesson, took one look at him, and dropped onto the piano bench. "You know what my cousin told me? She's at music school. She said research on expert performers found that how someone practices matters more than simply playing a piece many times." She shrugged. "So stop playing the whole song."

Ryder lowered the trumpet. "Then what do I practice?"

"Wherever it breaks. Just that."

He looked at his sheet music. The crack lived in four measures, sixteen through twenty, every single time. He'd been running from it, playing the easy parts over and over because they felt good. That was the pattern, now that he stared straight at it. He took a breath that filled his whole chest, set his feet, and played only those four measures. Slowly. It cracked anyway. He played them again, slower, watching his fingers on the valves, feeling where his air went thin. On the fifth try the G came out round and full, and the bell of the trumpet buzzed warm against his hands.

For twenty minutes he worked nothing but those measures, then added one measure before and one after, then two, then four, until the dangerous spot was stitched into the music around it. His mouth was wrecked, but he'd found the loose board and nailed it down. On the last run-through of the whole piece, measure twenty arrived like any other measure, smooth, almost boring, and Ryder almost laughed out loud. Mr. Clarke poked his head in from the hallway and raised an eyebrow.

"Do that again," Mr. Clarke said.

Ryder lifted the trumpet, gave one assertive nod, and played the passage clean.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
The bleachers at the rink were cold enough that Harper kept her mittens on inside her coat, which made her look like a camouflage-colored marshmallow, according to Syeda, who said it every single practice. Between periods of her brother's game, Manraj spread a folded sheet of baseball stats across three seats and jabbed his finger at one line.

"Estevez is ranked ninety-third in the league," he said. "Ninety-third. That's a crime."

Harper leaned over. "Who's Estevez?"

"Only the best hitter nobody talks about." Manraj tapped the column of batting averages. "See, the average is hits divided by official at-bats. And walks don't count as at-bats. So Estevez gets zero credit for all the times he worked a walk and got on base anyway. Ninety-three. It's like the ranking can't see half of what he does."

Syeda pulled her hat down. "You've explained this four times since October."

"Because it's still true."

Harper looked at the sheet. At the top, a player named Okafor had a higher average than Estevez, so the ranking put him higher. But in the column beside it, Estevez had a pile of walks, and Okafor had almost none. She did a rough count on her mitten, then pulled the mitten off with her teeth and used a pen from her coat.

"Okay," she said. "Official at-bats only. If Estevez had the exact same hits and at-bats as Okafor, but the walks got left out of the average, then Okafor looks better even though Estevez reaches base more." She flipped the pen in her hand. "So the ranking isn't measuring who gets on base. It's measuring who gets hits."

Manraj pointed at her with a nacho. "Yes. Thank you."

"So your guy isn't underrated," Harper said. "He's mismeasured. Different problem."

Manraj chewed on that along with the nacho. "That's worse."

"Wait, wait," Syeda said, sitting up. "If his average can fluctuate whenever he walks a bunch and it doesn't move the number at all, then one lucky week of hits could jump him forty spots. The ranking rewards streaks, not patience." She took the pen and circled two names near the top. "This guy is ranked sixth and he swings at everything. Estevez could be better and the chart would never say so."

Down on the ice, Harper's brother got called for tripping, and her mother stood up with the assertive posture of a person about to yell at a teenager in stripes. Ms. Yilmaz, who ran the snack bar and refereed on weekends, skated over to the penalty box instead and pointed the boy into it without a word.

Manraj folded his stats sheet. "I'm writing a letter to the league."

"About a baseball stat? At a hockey rink?"

"Truth doesn't care about the venue," Manraj said, and held the sheet up like a hall pass. "Estevez walks, therefore the number lies."

Syeda snatched the pen back. "First we count how many walks Okafor's got. If it's more than I think, your whole letter collapses."

"Then count fast," Manraj said, "my nachos are getting cold."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Subtracting an element's atomic number from an atom's mass number gives the number of neutrons, because the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
story:
Brielle tapped her pencil against the periodic table taped to the lab bench, where the symbols marched across the wall in their little boxes like seats in a stadium. Mr. Bianchi had promised a quiz on Friday, and Friday was tomorrow. She could find an element's box, sure, and she knew the big bold number had something to do with what the element was, but every time she tried the practice sheet, her answers came out wrong and she could not say why.

At the next bench, Soleil was quietly tearing the corner off her own paper, the way she did when the work got ahead of her. Arno noticed too, and slid his spare calculator down the bench without a word. Soleil mouthed "thanks" and kept her eyes down.

"Try carbon," Arno said to Brielle, because he had watched her pencil stalling for five minutes. "Carbon's easy. Atomic number six, mass number twelve."

"Six, twelve," Brielle repeated. She wrote both numbers in the margin. She knew the atomic number was six, and she knew the mass number was twelve, and she knew the quiz would ask for protons and neutrons, and somewhere between the knowing and the writing her brain snagged. Then she stared at the two numbers sitting side by side and something shifted. Six from twelve. She drew a small arrow between them. "Wait. If the atomic number is the protons, and six from twelve is six, then carbon has six neutrons."

"Is that how it works?" Soleil leaned over, forgettiing to hide her torn corner.

"Mass number counts protons plus neutrons," Brielle said slowly, testing each word as she said it. "So if I take the protons back out, what's left has to be the neutrons. Mass number minus atomic number." She flipped the sheet over and tried oxygen next, then sodium, her pencil moving faster each time. Her scratch paper filled up with little subtraction problems, testimony to how many tries it had taken her to trust the pattern.

Mr. Bianchi wandered past their bench on his rounds and glanced at the flipped paper without breaking stride. "That's authentic thinking, not memorizing," he said, and kept walking.

"Okay, so tomorrow I can actually participate instead of staring at the wall like it owes me money," Brielle said. She copied the rule into the margin of her notes, boxed it twice, then slid the paper across so Soleil could see the oxygen problem worked out start to finish. "You try sodium. I'll check you."

Soleil picked up her pencil, and Arno angled his periodic table so both of them could see it at once.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
The clock on Ms. Eze's wall ticked louder than a clock should, and George studied it so he would not have to study her. He had fallen asleep in geography twice this week, and once in math, and the school had sent him here with a pass he had crumpled into his pocket like evidence.

"So," said Ms. Eze, settling into the chair across from him. "Two weeks of falling asleep in class. That's a pattern. Any idea what's behind it?" George shrugged. "I'm just tired." She waited, which he hated, because waiting made room for the truth. "Sometimes tiredness isn't really about sleep," she went on. "Sometimes it's stress, or anxiety that stays switched on. Part of coping is figuring out what's actually going on." He kept his eyes on the clock. She was guessing in the wrong direction, and he let her.

Because yesterday, in the library, he had found out what was actually going on. A folded printout had fallen out of his jacket, one he was pretty sure his mom had tucked there after the doctor's visit she had dragged him to on Monday. He smoothed it open under the table while Emma-Rose pretended to read about volcanoes and Jakub stole her chips. The page was about cortisol. "Cortisol," Jakub had said, peering over George's shoulder. "Weird word." The paper said it was a hormone made by the adrenal glands, and that it rose during stress. Then came the line George had read three times: when stress lasted a long time, cortisol could stay high. Emma-Rose had frowned at it. "So weeks of stress keep it high? That's why the doctor thinks you've been so run down?" George had folded the page back along its creases and said nothing, because the thing that was keeping his stress switched on was not something you said out loud in a library.

That was the part he could not tell Ms. Eze either. His dad had gone for heart tests at the start of the month, and for three weeks the house had run on whispered phone calls and his mom's pretend-smile. George had stopped doing homework, lost all motivation for basketball tryouts, turned pessimistic about everything, and slept worse each night, which now made a strange kind of sense. His body had been staying braced the whole time, even while he told himself he was fine. "Here's what I'm thinking," Ms. Eze said, pulling him back to the office, to the ticking clock. "We could coordinate a plan. Shorter assignments, a quiet spot at lunch, a check-in with me once a week." She slid a blank page toward him. "But only if you tell me what we're planning around."

George looked at the blank page, then out the window, then at the phone in his pocket where a message had been sitting since seven that morning, from his dad, unread because he had been too scared to open it. He took the phone out. "Can I read something first?" he asked. He opened the message, and his whole chest let go at once. "Tests all clear," his dad had written. "Home by six. Order pizza." George turned the screen toward Ms. Eze. "It's my dad," he said. "He's okay."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
story:
Isabella stood at the pharmacy counter in her pajama pants and rain boots, because her mother had refused to let her stay home alone with a fever and no cough syrup. The fluorescent lights made everything look slightly green, including Ms. Bear, the pharmacist, who was building an intricate tower of prescription boxes behind the register. Isabella's head pounded, her list was compressed onto a scrap of receipt paper in handwriting that got worse toward the bottom, and all she wanted was to go home and sleep until Saturday.

"Flu, huh," said the woman ahead of her, glancing back with the pitying look people reserve for the contagious. "My whole office has it."

Isabella's mind, slow and sticky as it was, snagged on something. She had been fine last Tuesday. On Tuesday night she was at Leona's sleepover, crammed into a nest of sleeping bags with Leona and Eden, watching movies and passing one bowl of popcorn around until midnight. Wednesday she was fine too. Thursday morning she woke up feeling like she'd been hit by a truck. She turned the timeline over and over while the line inched forward. Two days. It had to have been Tuesday.

But nobody at the sleepover had been sick. Eden had sneezed twice, but Eden sneezed at everything, cats, dust, cold air. Leona had been the healthiest of them, doing cartwheels in the hallway at ten p.m. And then, Thursday afternoon, Leona had texted her: "I'm so sick, mom says it's the flu." Isabella had felt sorry for her and thought nothing of it.

When she got home, she called Leona instead of texting, because a theory deserved a voice. "When did you start feeling it?" she asked, coughing into her sleeve.

"Thursday morning, same as you," Leona said, nasal and miserable. "I was totally fine at the sleepover, though. I felt great."

"That's the thing," Isabella said slowly, testing each word like a step on ice. "Ms. Bear had this flyer at the counter, about flu. People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms. So Wednesday, all day, you were giving it to everybody and didn't know."

There was a silence on the line, the kind that meant someone was rearranging their memory. "The popcorn bowl," Leona said finally. "We all ate from the popcorn bowl."

"The popcorn bowl."

Leona groaned. "I have to call Eden." She paused, and her voice got small. "I really did feel fine, Isabella. I didn't do it on purpose."

"I know," Isabella said, and meant it. "That's the worst part, kind of. Nobody did anything wrong and we're all sick anyway."

"Eden's going to be so mad," Leona said. "She has the regional meet on Saturday." The call clicked off, and Isabella sat looking at her untouched homework, her cold soup, the empty bowl on her desk that still smelled faintly of butter. Then she picked up the phone and texted Eden herself: check your temperature tonight, and I'm sorry, it probably came from us.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Alexandre spread his pencils across the wobbliest table in the dilapidated corner of the public library, the one by the cracked window where the radiator grumbled all winter. He was drawing a poster for the seventh-grade art contest, a knight on a cliff with a banner snapping overhead, and the deadline was Friday. So far the knight looked like he was standing in the middle of a very boring parking lot.

Lilianne dropped into the chair across from him with three books about famous painters and the last cookie from the vending machine. "The knight's dead center," she said, chewing. "That's why it feels like a flyer for a dentist's office."

"Rude," said Alexandre, but she was right, and he knew it. He had moved the knight left, right, and up and down, and every version still felt flat. He pushed the drawing aside and stared at the window instead, at the snowbank outside.

Malak arrived next, out of breath, waving a photography magazine he'd found on the returns cart. "Look at this. Every good photo in here has the subject off to the side, and a lot of them have it at a spot about a third of the way across." He flipped pages fast. "Sunset here, dog there, bridge there."

Alexandre grabbed a pencil and, on the margin of his poster, drew a rectangle split into three columns and three rows, a simple grid of nine boxes. Where the lines crossed, he made small dots. "It's called the rule of thirds," Malak read from the magazine. "It says you put your main subject along those lines or where they cross."

The logic of it hit Alexandre like the radiator kicking on. He taped fresh paper over his botched draft and redrew the knight so the figure sat right along the left vertical line, the sword tip touching one of the crossing points, the banner sweeping across the top third. He put the castle small in the bottom right, near another crossing point. Lilianne leaned in and went quiet, which for her was a standing ovation.

Ms. McKenzie, the librarian, stopped behind them with her cart of returns. "That one's coming along," she said. Then she squinted at the knight's helmet, which Alexandre had accidentally drawn with two visors, one above the other, like a helmet wearing a smaller helmet. "Is he prepared for a second battle?"

"He's got eyes in the back of his head," said Alexandre. "Survival adaptation."

Malak laughed so hard he knocked over the pencil cup, and forty pencils radiated across the floor in every direction, a perfect demonstration of everything the rule of thirds was not. Alexandre dove under the table to gather them and came up grinning, holding his poster to the light.

"Friday," Lilianne said. "First prize is a real set of markers."

"Second prize is a set of markers wearing a smaller set of markers," said Alexandre, and he got back to work, sword tip planted exactly on the crossing point.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Riley had been checking the family group chat all afternoon, mostly to escape the fact that tonight was his first school dance. His mom kept sending reminders about the ticket, and his older sister had sent one message: "Don't stand by the speakers, dork." Riley had ignored that, until he got curious and looked up whether standing by speakers was actually a thing. He found a page from some safety agency. Eighty-five decibels was safe for eight hours a day, the page said, and every time the sound got three decibels louder, the safe time was cut in half. He did the math on his fingers on the bus to the gym. If the speakers were way louder than that, the safe time could shrink to almost nothing.

The gym was already thumping when he walked in with Neil and Kate. Streamers hung from the basketball hoops, and the dance floor was sparse at first, just a few eighth graders shuffling near the middle. Riley checked his phone one last time. His mom had texted, "Have fun, be kind," and his sister had texted, "Loser." He pocketed the phone.

Neil headed straight for the wall of speakers stacked beside the stage. "Best spot," he shouted, planting himself a foot away. Riley followed, but after two songs his ears had that pressed, fluttering feeling, like when a plane descends. He swallowed, and something in his hearing did a strange reflex click. He remembered the halving rule and started counting in his head. If it was ninety-one decibels over there, that was two halvings, which meant two hours. If it was louder, less. The numbers piled up faster than he liked.

"Let's move back," he said to Neil.

Neil shook his head. "It's better here."

Kate touched her own ear and winced. "Actually, my ears feel weird. Like full." That settled it, sort of. Riley walked ten steps back and stood there, and after a minute the pressure in his ears faded. He couldn't see the decibels, and he couldn't see the safe time draining out of Neil either, but he could test it. He walked back beside the speakers for one song, felt the flutter return, walked away again, and felt it fade. Same result twice. Distance was doing something real.

"Neil, come here for one song," he called. "Trust me, then go back if you want."

Neil scowled but shuffled over. A slow song came on, and the three of them stood in a loose triangle at the edge of the floor. Neil rolled his shoulders. "Okay, it's nicer back here. I'm not saying you were right."

"You kind of are," Kate said. She held out her hand to Neil, then, after a beat, to Riley, half daring him to take it.

Riley looked at her palm, then at the speakers glowing far across the gym.

"Fine," he said, "but only for the quiet songs."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Jasmine sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with her mom's laptop, a notebook, and two cookies she was pretending were a balanced breakfast. Her assignment was due Monday: survey the class, then build a spreadsheet with a formula that added a column and a bar chart to show the results. She had the survey numbers already. Asees averaged 14 hours a week of gaming, Sargun averaged 13, and Jasmine herself clocked in at a tragic 9, which she planned to symbolize with the smallest, most dignified bar the software would allow.

First she typed the numbers into a column, then hunted through the menus until she found the formula bar. She typed "=SUM(" and selected the column, held her breath, and pressed Enter. The total appeared like magic: 36. She actually pumped her fist, which felt radical for a Tuesday morning. "I am a spreadsheet wizard," she announced to the toaster.

The chart took longer. She clicked Insert, picked a bar chart, and stared at the result. Asees's bar towered over hers like a skyscraper over a garden shed. The gap looked enormous, like Asees was a pro gamer and Jasmine was close to extinction as a gamer at all. She screenshotted it and texted it to Sargun, who replied within seconds: "WOW. Asees is destroying us. Also why is your bar basically flat?"

Jasmine squinted at the chart. Something felt off. She remembered a flashback from last weekend: her neighbour Ms. Ho had shown her a bar chart about bird populations in the neighbourhood park, and Jasmine had gasped that one species had practically vanished. Ms. Ho had laughed and pointed at the tiny numbers along the side. "The axis starts at eight," she'd said. "Not zero." Jasmine hadn't really understood then, but now she leaned toward the laptop screen and checked the numbers along her own chart's side. They started at eight, too.

She had an idea. If the bars only had to stretch from eight upward, then 14 and 9 wouldn't look that different. It was worth testing. She right-clicked the axis, poked around until she found a setting for the minimum value, and typed 0. The chart redrew itself instantly. Asees's bar was still the tallest, sure, but Jasmine's bar was nearly three quarters of it. The "enormous gap" had shrunk into a small lead. She laughed out loud. The chart hadn't lied, exactly, but it had stretched the truth like taffy.

She texted the new chart to Sargun with the message "plot twist." Then she thought about what to do with her assignment. Ms. Ho's bird chart had started above zero, and so did half the charts in her science textbook, and she was pretty sure her cousin's favourite sports channel did it constantly to make one team's tiny lead look like a crushing victory. Jasmine opened her notebook and wrote "tricky charts" at the top of a fresh page. Maybe she would hand in both versions of her gaming chart. Maybe she would title it something dramatic, like "The Great Bar Chart Deception." The cursor blinked at her, waiting, and she cracked her knuckles.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
Quinn stood at the white line near the first turn, hands on her knees, while Ms. Shevchenko clicked her stopwatch and told her to go again. The first attempt had been a disaster. Quinn had sprinted the opening like it was a hundred-metre dash, thrown everything into the final stretch, and then discovered there was a whole other lap left. She had jogged the last two hundred metres with her lungs burning while Greyson, running beside her, kept shouting, "One more lap! You've got one more lap!" Now she needed to retrieve her water bottle from the fence and figure out what had gone wrong.

"It's exactly two laps," Greyson said as she drank. "The track's four hundred metres, the race is eight hundred, so it's two of them. Two, not one."

"But the finish line was right there," Quinn said. "I saw it."

"That was the start of your second lap, not the end of your race."

Quinn turned that over. The problem wasn't her legs, which felt strong, and it wasn't the line itself, which was just paint. The problem was invisible: her own brain deciding the race was over when it was only half done. If she couldn't see the difference, she needed a way to feel it. She crouched at the line and made a plan she could actually test. First lap, she would hold back, imagine a leash on her speed, and let Jaycob pull ahead if he wanted to. Only when she crossed the line a second time would she let go.

Ms. Shevchenko blew the whistle. Jaycob shot out like a firework, and Quinn's whole body screamed to chase him. She counted her steps instead, kept her arms low and loose, and told herself the ache of holding back was the leash doing its job. The other runners stretched into a thin string, and she stayed at the back of it, running what felt absurdly slow. When she swept through the finish line the first time, her legs begged to kick. She held on. One more lap.

Then she passed the line again, and this time it meant something different. Quinn let the leash out. She found a gear she hadn't known she had, hauled past Jaycob on the back turn, and crossed the real finish with her chest heaving and her time almost fifteen seconds faster than before. Ms. Shevchenko showed her the watch and actually smiled.

The cost came at the announcement board after practice. Jaycob had made the relay team, and Quinn's name was on the alternates list, because the coach wanted her fresh for the eight hundred at the meet. "You'll run it well," Jaycob said, and she knew he meant it, but his voice had a small flat spot in it. They walked off the track together, spikes hanging from their fingers, while the mowers droned across the field and the whole ecosystem of practice, balls and cones and shouting, packed itself away behind them.

"At the meet," Greyson called from the gate, "remember what you told yourself out there."

"Two laps," Quinn said. "First one easy, second one fast."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Kayla flopped onto her bed at 9:40 p.m. with her phone in one hand and her half-finished article in the other. The school paper wanted a piece on the swim team by midnight, and all she had was a ranking she'd screenshotted from the league site: Camille fourth, Meghan fifth. Her thumbs hovered over the group chat.

"How close were you and Meghan at regionals?" she typed.

Camille answered first. "Don't remind me. Fourth AGAIN. Might as well be last."

Meghan sent a shrugging emoji. "You beat me, that's all that matters."

Kayla stared at the ranking list. Fourth, fifth. Two lines, two names. But how far apart? She texted, "No, like, what were the actual times?"

The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Camille sent a photo of the official results sheet, crumpled but readable. Kayla pinched the screen to zoom. Camille's time and Meghan's time were different by eight hundredths of a second. But Meghan's time and the girl in sixth place were different by almost four seconds.

Kayla sat up. The ranking made them look evenly spaced, like rungs on a ladder, and they weren't even close to evenly spaced. Fourth and fifth were practically the same race; fifth and sixth were a different universe. She scrolled up and found the top of the sheet. First and second place differed by less than a hundredth of a second. First and third, by two full seconds.

"You lost the gold by a hundredth of a second?" she texted Camille.

"One one-hundredth," Camille replied. "I timed my blink afterward. Longer."

Kayla laughed out loud, alone in her room, then pulled her laptop over and started deleting paragraphs. She'd written "our swimmers are falling behind the leaders," which the times didn't actually say. Camille was a fingertip behind the fastest girl in the region. The numbers on the sheet said that; the ranking didn't. A ranking told you who was ahead, not by how much, and that distinction was the whole story.

At 10:55 she messaged the chat one more time. "Article says you basically tied for fourth and were a blink off first. Also I'm delegating the photo captions to whoever's still awake."

Meghan replied instantly, "Me. Send it."

Kayla hit send on the draft, then screenshot the results sheet and attached it with a caption: "Fourth place. By eight hundredths." Camille sent back three fire emojis and the message, "A blink off a medal. Print that."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Mr. Schneider set the microscope on the picnic table beside the barn and told the boys they could use it until the rain came. Daniel had brought the worksheet from science class, with its empty boxes marked cell wall, membrane, nucleus. He needed a perfect slide by Monday, and he felt it as an obligation, the kind that sat in his stomach until it was finished. Maxence had already peeled a fat slice from one of the onions in the crate, thick and juicy, and dropped it onto a glass slide.

Through the eyepiece there was nothing. Daniel turned the focus knob slowly, first one way, then the other, and saw only a grey darkness, like looking into a closed cupboard. "It's broken," Maxence said, peering over Daniel's shoulder. Japji took the eyepiece off, held it up to the sky, and announced that it worked fine. So it wasn't the microscope. It was the onion.

Daniel stood in the doorway of the barn and thought about the light. The lamp underneath the stage had to shine up through the sample, and a thick slab of onion would block all of it. He remembered the papery layer inside, the one that clung like wet tissue between the rings. He peeled a fresh onion apart, found that inner skin, and tugged free a piece as thin as breath. He laid it flat in a drop of water and lowered the cover slip.

Cells appeared like bricks in a wall, each one a tidy rectangle with a darker dot resting inside it. "There," Japji said. "The thin skin is only one cell thick, so the light goes right through it." Daniel drew what he saw, labeling the stiff outer edge of every rectangle as the cell wall, the faint line just inside it as the membrane, and the dark dot as the nucleus. He had always thought a cell would be something mysterious and hard to isolate, a single speck you had to hunt for, but here they were, dozens of them, arranged as neatly as tiles in Mr. Schneider's kitchen.

Maxence, who had spent the whole morning insisting science was boring, took over the microscope and refused to give it back. He started experimenting on his own, isolating skins from different onions, from a shallot, and finally from a fat purple bulb Mr. Schneider said came from a tropical variety he'd ordered on a whim.

"Look at this one," Maxence said, not looking up. "The walls are purple too. Every single one." Daniel leaned in beside him as the first drops of rain began to tap the barn roof.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
Mackenzie stood in front of the hallway mirror for the third time and pulled the scarf off her neck again. Her mom appeared behind her with a laundry basket on one hip. "Incorporate the scarf," her mom said. "It pulls the whole thing together."

"It itches."

"It's a dance, not a camping trip." Her mom went on sorting towels, and Mackenzie looped the scarf around once, loosely, where it couldn't touch her collarbone. In the garage, her dad had the car hood up and was wiping grease off his hands. "Piston's seized," he called through the door. "Have fun. Text when you're home."

Veer arrived at six with a garment bag and a hair straightener, like the dance was a prestigious award ceremony instead of the first-ever fall social in the gym. Jax showed up last, still in his school hoodie, hands in his pockets. "Ready," he said, and that was all any of them said about it in the car.

The gym had a DJ booth stacked with speakers taller than Mr. Hernández, who stood by the door collecting tickets and plugging his ears with one finger whenever the bass dropped. Mackenzie danced with Veer near the middle of the floor. Jax disappeared into the crowd by the wall of speakers, and every time she looked over, he was closer to them, nodding along like he was part of the equipment.

The next morning, Mackenzie was eating cereal when someone knocked. It was Jax, hood up, and Veer behind him. "Still ringing," Jax said. "Since last night. Like a TV that won't turn off."

Mackenzie set down her spoon. "Mine stopped when I got home." She looked at Veer, who shook her head. "Mine too. So why yours?"

She counted it out on the table. "We were in the same gym. Same music. Same three hours." She tapped Jax's spot on the imaginary floor. "You were standing right against the speakers."

Jax shrugged. "It's just ringing. It goes away."

"Does it?" She pulled her dad's phone over and typed, scrolling past ads for hearing aids until she found it, then read it out loud. "It's called tinnitus." She kept reading. "It says ringing after loud music is a warning sign. It means the noise was loud enough to damage hearing."

The kitchen went quiet except for the drip from the faucet. Jax took his hood down and rubbed one ear, then the other, like he could wipe the sound out.

"So it's a warning," Veer said slowly. "Not just an annoyance."

"Where were you standing?" Mackenzie asked him.

"By the speakers. All night." Jax looked at the phone screen, then at the window, and shoved his hands back in his pockets. "Next dance, I'm on the far side of the DJ."

"Take the scarf," Mackenzie's mom said from the doorway, holding it out. "You can incorporate it over your ears."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: A river cuts downward mainly because the sand, pebbles and boulders it carries grind against its bed, a process called abrasion.
story:
The planetarium's newest exhibit was called "Canyons of Mars," but Alexandra barely glanced at the red photographs on the wall. She was crouched beside the river table, a long shallow tank where water hissed over a bed of sand and gravel, and in her palm she held a stone so smooth it felt like soap. Joseph had dared her to figure out where it came from, and Mr. Bui, who ran the place, had smiled in that annoying way adults smile when they know something you don't.

"Ten minutes," Joseph said, checking the clock above the exit. "Then you have to present. Like a tour guide." He and Omar had appointed themselves her audience, which was worse than having strangers, because strangers wouldn't heckle.

Alexandra turned the stone under the tank's lights. It was oval, rounded on every side, with no sharp edge anywhere. A rock broken off a cliff would be jagged, she thought, the way a snapped chocolate bar is jagged. So something had worn this one down, patiently, over a time she couldn't see. The river, obviously. But how? Water alone felt too soft, like a sponge trying to sand a table. She dropped the stone into the current and watched it tumble downstream, knocking against the gravel, spinning, grinding.

That was when she saw it. The moving water wasn't empty. It carried sand, and pebbles, and even a few small boulders, all dragging along the bottom of the tank, and everywhere they rolled, the sand bed beneath them was being scraped into a shallow channel. The channel deepened, drop by drop, and the sides of it stayed steep, like a tiny canyon. It wasn't the water alone. The river's own load of sediment was doing the cutting.

She looked up at the tall poster near the exit, the one with a heroic astronaut and the words OUR FUTURE IS UPWARD, and snorted. "That thing's pure propaganda," she said. "It's from some old campaign. It's trying to intimidate you into agreeing with it."

"Focus," Omar said. "Your ten minutes are almost up."

Alexandra cupped the stone again, feeling how vulnerable its smoothness seemed now, the product of so much grinding. When Mr. Bui drifted over, she held it out to him. "The river cut this channel because of the sand and pebbles it carries, grinding against the bed," she said. "It's called abrasion. That's what polished my stone, too. Over millions of years, that same grinding carves a whole canyon."

Mr. Bui's smile changed shape. He picked up the stone, weighed it in his hand, and set it gently back in the current at the deepest point of the little channel, where the water took it and rolled it on downstream.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Harper had one goal before the bell: make the computer add the money column by itself and turn it into a bar chart. The science club was selling tropical plant seedlings, orchids and little pineapple starts, to pay for a class terrarium, and she had promised Mr. Zhou a chart of who had sold what. She typed her first formula into the spreadsheet and pressed Enter.

#VALUE! flashed in the cell like an alarm.

"That's not a sum," said Pierre, leaning over from the next computer. "That's a complaint."

Harper glared at the screen. She had written =SUM(A2:A9), and it should have worked, so something hidden was wrong, some rule she couldn't see. She clicked into A4, the cell for Brayden's sales, and there it was: he had typed "12 dollars" instead of just 12. The letters were poisoning the math. She deleted the word, kept the number, and pressed Enter again. The total jumped from an error to a real answer, 87.

"Okay, now the chart," she said, heart drumming. She highlighted the names and the numbers, clicked Insert, chose bar chart, and the columns rose up on the screen, Brayden's tall and green at the front. Brayden himself came jogging over from the printer and pumped both fists.

"Grandpa's going to lose his mind," Harper said. "He told me last night that when he was young, he had to do columns of sums with a pencil and an adding machine. Then VisiCalc came out, and it was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it ran on the Apple II in 1979. He said people bought the computer just to get the program."

"Wait, it was called VisiCalc?" Pierre asked, copying the word into his notes.

"That's the one." Harper couldn't stop grinning. "He said he felt like he'd opposed a dictator, the adding machine, and won."

Mr. Zhou circled the lab, pausing behind her chair. He studied the chart for a long moment.

"Terrarium money," Harper said quickly. "I'll update it every Friday. You can count on me, it's my obligation as treasurer."

"Good," said Mr. Zhou. "Print it. I want it on the door by lunch."

The printer hummed and spat the page warm into her hands, Brayden's green tower standing tallest.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
Zachary had one Saturday and one plan: bake real bread for his parents' anniversary dinner, start to finish, all by himself. The wheat flour came from the miller's stall, and the honey from the jar Leilani was holding up to the light at the farmers' market like it was treasure.

"Smell this," she said. "Wildflower. Your kitchen is going to be amazing."

Zayan swung the flour bag over his shoulder and groaned. "If we don't hurry, amazing is going to evade us. Your parents get home at six, and you've never made bread in your life."

They had until six. It was already noon.

At Mr. Russo's produce stall, Zachary stopped. The old farmer was buying coffee from the vendor next door, and Zachary had heard a rumour that Mr. Russo's wife baked bread every week. He took the chance. "Sir, my dough always turns into a brick. My test loaf last week could have cracked a window."

Mr. Russo laughed. "How long did you knead it?"

"Knead? I stirred it until it looked mixed. Maybe a minute."

"Ask your grandmother about gluten," Mr. Russo said, counting out coins. "Or find out yourself. You have a whole afternoon."

Back in Zachary's kitchen, the flour went into the biggest vessel they owned, Mom's giant mixing bowl, and the water hit it in a rush. The recipe card, in his grandmother's handwriting, said ten minutes of kneading before the dough rises. Ten whole minutes. Zachary had always skipped past that, assuming mixing was kneading. Now he had a suspicion: the mixing wasn't the point. Something in the flour only woke up when it met water, and kneading made it stronger and stretchier. That thing was gluten, the word was right there on the card.

"Time me," he told Zayan, and started.

The first two minutes, the dough was ragged and sticky, and it clung to his fingers like it wanted to evade every fold he tried. At minute five it changed, smoothing out under his palms. By minute eight it was stretchy, snapping back when he pulled it, soft as an earlobe.

"It's alive," Leilani whispered, watching it rise near the warm oven. "It's actually puffing up."

The loaf went into the oven at five o'clock, golden and dome-shaped, filling the kitchen with a smell that made Zayan open the oven light three times just to look.

At ten to six, footsteps sounded on the front porch. The bread was still cooling, and Zachary was still holding the knife.

"Don't cut it, don't cut it, wait," Leilani hissed.

The door began to open.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in proportion to their share of the vote, so a party with 30 percent of the vote gets about 30 percent of the seats.
story:
The community centre smelled of floor wax and orange juice, and Audrey had claimed the big table by the window for her ballots. Ms. Santos-Reyes, who ran the youth council program, had handed out three hundred mock ballots from last week's vote, where four fictional parties had competed for ten council seats. Audrey's job was to recount them the first way, the way her school had always done it: the party with the most votes in each round wins the seat, and everyone else gets nothing. She sorted the slips into piles and started tallying. The Sunflower Party had won six seats, the Green Hats three, and the Rivers Party one, even though the Rivers pile looked almost as thick as the Green Hats pile.

"That seems off," Audrey said, fanning the ballots out across the table. "Rivers got way more votes than one seat's worth. I checked three times."

Cillian leaned over from the next table, where he was supposed to be tallying the same ballots a different way. "Mine looks totally different. I've got Sunflower with four seats, Green Hats with two, Rivers with three, and the Comet Party with one."

Mary dropped her pencil. "We counted the same ballots? That's impossible." She marched over and squinted at Cillian's tally sheet, then at Audrey's. Both sheets listed the same vote counts at the top. Sunflower, thirty-nine percent. Green Hats, twenty-one percent. Rivers, thirty percent. Comet, ten percent.

"Wait," Audrey said slowly, tracing her finger down Cillian's column. "Sunflower has thirty-nine percent of the votes and four seats out of ten. Rivers has thirty percent and three seats." She grabbed a scrap paper and wrote the numbers side by side. Under Cillian's method, the seats roughly matched the share of the vote. A party with thirty percent of the vote got about thirty percent of the seats. Under her own first method, Sunflower's thirty-nine percent of the votes had turned into sixty percent of the seats, and Rivers' thirty percent had collapsed into ten percent of them. "It's like the first method takes a small lead and stretches it," she said. "The second one keeps the proportions."

"That's the one Ms. Santos-Reyes called proportional representation," Cillian said. "I wrote it at the top. See?" He pointed at his heading, and Audrey copied the words onto her scrap paper.

Ms. Santos-Reyes drifted past with a stack of juice cups. "Find something interesting?" she asked, and Audrey slid both tally sheets toward her.

"The same ballots gave us two different councils," Audrey said. "Under the first one, Rivers gets one seat. Under proportional representation, they get three. And I want to know why anyone would pick the first way at all." She paused, then added, "Though I guess I only understand half of it. The rest is still vague to me, like how they'd decide things if no party had a majority."

"Good question," said Ms. Santos-Reyes, and kept walking, which Audrey chose to interpret as go find out.

"Next Saturday," Audrey announced, pulling the ballots back into a stack, "we run a vote with real parties, and we recount it both ways in front of everybody. Commerce at the snack table, speeches at the podium, the whole thing." She looked at Cillian. "Can your group handle the proportional count while mine does the first one?"

Cillian was already drawing a fresh tally sheet. "Six columns," he said, "and room for a recount."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
Mrs. Hollis's living room smelled like lavender and old magazines, and a lizard named Duke was staring at Noah from a tank beside the couch. "He's a carnivore," she said as she pulled on her coat. "Crickets, twice a week. The box is in the fridge, which is either brilliant or horrifying." Noah nodded like he took notes, which he did not, because he was too busy memorizing where the sippy cups lived. Then the front door opened a crack and a small person named Ruby, age three, sprinted in wearing one sock and a dinosaur helmet.

"Wait," Noah said, just as Mrs. Hollis reached for the handle. "What's your address here?" She blinked at him. "In case I call 911," he went on, feeling his ears go warm. "I heard they ask for the address first, so it's probably good to have it ready." She recited it slowly, and he wrote it on a sticky note and pressed it to the table right beside the phone. "Smart," she said, and then, "Bedtime is eight, snacks are in the basket, do not let her talk you into three snacks," and she was gone.

Ruby talked him into two snacks, which Noah decided was the equivalent of a victory, since he'd braced for three. She fed a corner of her cracker to Duke, who ignored it with the dignity of a true meat-eater, and she laughed so hard she snorted. Then, during an enthusiastic dinosaur-helmet head shake, she bonked her forehead on the coffee table. Noah winced at the sound, hollow as a drum, and Ruby's face did the slow crumple before the wailing started.

He checked her forehead, which had a pink mark but no lump forming yet, and she stopped crying the second he offered a frozen blueberry "ice pack." Still, his stomach kept doing somersaults. What if she got dizzy later? What if that was a thing that happened? He decided the safest move was to call and ask, so he picked up the phone, sticky note in hand, and dialed 911. The dispatcher answered, and before he'd said more than "Hi, this isn't exactly an emergency," she asked for the address of the emergency. He read it straight off the note, quick as anything, and felt the somersaults settle.

"We're fine," he explained. "She bumped her head, there's no bump, she's eating a blueberry, I just wanted to check about dizzy." The dispatcher told him what to watch for and said calling was the right thing to do. When Mrs. Hollis came home at nine, she found Ruby asleep in the dinosaur helmet and Noah on the couch with the sticky note still in his hand. "Busy night?" she asked. He held up the note. "Your address saved the day," he said, and Duke, watching from his tank, blinked one eye, like a tiny scaly witness who would never tell.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
Alexis stood at the corner of Maple and Third with her sketchbook, trying to figure out why her drawing looked wrong. In art room that morning, Ms. Grant had set them a project: draw a street scene, and the class would nominate the best one for the hallway display. Alexis wanted that spot on the wall more than she wanted almost anything else. Back in the art room, her prototype had looked fine, with every slanted line running toward one dot on the page. But standing here, at the actual corner, the real street refused to cooperate. The building across from her showed its whole side, windows marching along it, and no single dot on her paper could collect all those lines.

"You've been staring at that corner for ten minutes," said Abbey, who had walked over with Lianna after soccer practice. "What's wrong with it?"

"Everything slants different ways," Alexis said. "Watch." She held up her sketchbook, then pointed at the brick building. "In my drawing, all the lines go to one vanishing point. Out here, they don't. I thought I broke perspective."

Lianna leaned against the traffic sign and squinted down Third Street. "Down there it works, though. Look straight down the street and it's like the road narrows to a dot. Turn your head toward the corner and it stops doing that."

Alexis tried it. Facing straight down Third, she could see it: the fronts of the houses faced her, flat and square, while their sides squeezed inward toward one faraway point. Her pencil lines could all run there and the picture made sense. But the moment she turned to look at the corner itself, the building's face and its side spread apart, each going its own direction, and the single dot idea fell apart.

"So it's not broken," Alexis said slowly, flipping to a new page. "One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street. The fronts of things face you, and everything else goes back to that one point. At the corner you're not facing straight down anything. That's why my drawing lied."

She planted herself in the middle of the sidewalk, facing dead ahead down Third, and started over. She kept the proportions of the near house big, drew the fronts of the buildings as flat shapes facing her, and ran every receding line toward her vanishing point. Abbey and Lianna stood behind her, spotting windows and doorways she could name from memory. The page filled fast, and this time when Alexis held it up beside the real street, the two matched.

Monday in the art room, Ms. Grant pinned the drawings along the chalkboard. When Alexis's street went up, Abbey's hand shot into the air. "I nominate that one."

"Seconded," said Lianna.

Ms. Grant smiled and reached for the pushpins. "Wall, by the door."

Alexis grinned at her two friends and slid her eraser back into her pencil case.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: Defenders can answer a pick by switching, meaning the two defenders trade the players they are guarding.
story:
Ethan stood at the top of the key with the ball sweating in his hands, trying to remember everything at once. Mr. Romano had given him the point guard job two weeks ago, and every practice since then had ended with the same frustrated whistle. "Call something," the coach kept saying, and Ethan kept freezing, because calling a play meant knowing what five other people would do before they did it. Today, though, he had a plan, and a reason for it. He had spent lunch watching the seventh-grade team on tape, and he had noticed something odd: whenever their guard came off a big teammate's screen, a different defender seemed to be waiting for him, every single time. Ethan suspected there was a rule behind it, not luck, and he wanted to test the idea on Christian and Felipe in the school gym.

The gym smelled like floor wax and old sneakers. Half the ceiling fans were boxed up because the district planned to renovate the place over the summer, and Felipe kept glancing up at them like the spinning blades might fall. "Focus," Ethan said, tapping the ball. "Felipe, you set the screen on my defender. Christian, you stay in the corner and watch." Felipe planted his wide feet beside Ethan's defender, and Ethan rubbed his shoulder off the screen, exactly the way the tape showed.

The trouble came instantly. Felipe's man stepped over and slid in front of Ethan, arms out, waiting. Ethan pulled up, confused, then ran the whole thing again to be sure. Same result. He came around the screen and found the tall defender there instead of his own man, while his own man had peeled off to guard Felipe, who was now standing open by the basket. Ethan's stomach did a flip, the good kind. It wasn't a mistake. It was the answer.

"They switched," Ethan said, spinning the ball on one finger. "When Felipe screens, they trade the guys they're guarding. My defender takes Felipe, Felipe's defender takes me."

Christian, who had been quiet in the corner for ten minutes, finally spoke up. "Great. So you score and the rest of us just set furniture." His voice had an edge, and Ethan finally heard it. Christian hadn't touched the ball once all week. He was always the one spacing out to the corner while Ethan and Felipe got the glory, and Ethan had been too busy worrying about his own new job to notice.

So on the next possession, Ethan changed the play. "Felipe, screen, then roll to the hoop," he called, and when the defenders traded their men again, Ethan drove two steps, drew Felipe's old defender toward the ball, and lofted a soft pass over the top. Felipe caught it and laid it in off the glass. Christian pumped his fist from the corner, then jogged over grinning. "Okay, run it again, but this time I'll screen and roll," he said. "My uncle played point guard, so it's basically hereditary." Ethan laughed and inbounded the ball, and this time he pointed at Christian first.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
The dining hall smelled like pancakes and bug spray, and Nathaniel had not touched either. He pushed his fork through a puddle of syrup while campers at the long tables shouted jokes he didn't understand yet. This was his first morning away from home, ever, and he'd already lost something: the compass his grandfather had given him, the little brass one with the chip in the case.

"Check your bunk again," said April, who sat across from him and seemed to know how everything at Camp Wenlock worked. "Things show up."

"It's porous up here," Nathaniel said, tapping his temple. "Stuff falls out of my head, never mind my bunk."

Philip leaned over from the next table. "Nothing falls out of a head. The skull's solid except little holes for nerves. It's the ear you have to worry about. That's mostly cartilage, not even bone."

"That is not comforting," Nathaniel said.

At the far end of the hall, Mr. Le rattled a spoon against a juice glass. "Tonight," he announced, "the whole cabin goes to the dock for lights-out. No phones allowed. If you can't find north out there, you sleep with the mosquitoes."

The cabins hooted and groaned. Nathaniel's stomach dropped. Without his compass, without a phone, north could be anywhere.

That afternoon he searched the swimming area, the path to the washhouse, even under the porous rubber mats by the canoe rack, but the brass compass was gone for good. He considered trying to salvage a piece of it from his memory instead: his grandfather, the last night before camp, pointing at a picture in a star book. Something about a ladle. Nathaniel had been half listening, packing his duffel, and the words had slipped through him like water.

At ten o'clock the cabins lay down on the dock, boards still warm from the sun, and the sky over the lake went black and crowded. "Okay, genius," Philip whispered. "Which way's north?"

Nathaniel sat up. Somewhere above the tree line hung a cluster of seven stars shaped like a ladle with a bent handle. He remembered his grandfather tapping the picture, the two stars on the far side of the bowl, the ones at the outer edge. "The two stars on the edge of the bowl," he said slowly, "the pointer stars, they're called. Grandpa said they point at the North Star. Polaris."

"So follow them," April said.

Nathaniel raised his arm and drew a line with his finger, from the bottom outer star through the top one, out into the empty dark. Five lengths of the bowl, his grandfather had said with his hands, but Nathaniel's arm found it on its own: one star sitting almost alone, brighter than the others around it, exactly where his finger landed.

"That one," he said. "Polaris, the North Star. North is straight out over the water."

"Then I get the end of the dock away from the mosquitoes," Philip said, already rolling.

Nathaniel lay back down and kept his eyes on the star until Mr. Le's flashlight swept the dock. The compass was still gone, but he didn't reach for his pocket the way he'd done all day.

"Still awake, Nathaniel?" Mr. Le asked softly.

"Just fixing north in my head," Nathaniel said. "It's not going anywhere now."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A climate graph usually shows each month's average temperature as a line and each month's average rainfall as bars on the same chart.
story:
The trail climbed through pinon pines until the trees thinned and the land opened into dry, cracked earth. Mr. Çelik stopped the group where a small sign showed the edge of a research plot, and he pulled folded papers from his pack.

"Field exercise," he said. "Each of you gets a climate graph for a different place. Match your graph to a spot along this trail, and tell me why it fits."

Kayla unfolded her paper. The chart had twelve tall bars, one for each month, and a thin line curving across the top. She frowned. The bars were huge, some reaching past halfway up the page, and they dropped low in the middle months. "If the bars are temperature," she muttered, "this place is boiling in January and freezing in July. That makes no sense."

Jayda leaned over. "Mine has bars too." She held hers up. Jayda's bars were stubby, almost flat, while her line sat high and barely moved all year. Jayda's one goal this whole hike had been to prove her graph belonged somewhere hot, so she could claim the shady spot by the creek for lunch. "Mine is the desert, obviously. Look how flat everything is."

Bruce crouched on a rock, turning his paper sideways, then upside down. He wanted to find the answer before anyone else, because he had promised his little brother he would bring home something clever from this trip. "There are two things on the same chart," he said slowly. "So they can't both be temperature."

Kayla looked at the legend printed in the corner, small enough that she had skipped it the way she skipped the instructions on cereal boxes. The bars were labeled in millimeters. The line was labeled in degrees. "The bars are rainfall," she said. "The line is temperature." She read the axis again to be sure. "Every month's average rainfall is a bar, and every month's average temperature is that one line, on the same chart."

She stared at her own graph with new eyes. Twelve tall bars, drenched months stacked side by side, and a warm line that never dropped low. Jayda's paper showed the opposite, bars so short the place could consume almost nothing from the sky all year, with heat holding steady above them.

"So mine is a rainforest," Kayla said. "And yours, Jayda, that's a desert. Hot line, almost no rain." Jayda groaned and pointed at the cracked ground around them. "Then this is my spot for lunch. Deal with the sun."

Mr. Çelik was crouched beside a clump of waxy-leaved scrub, listening. "So which one grows here, then?" he asked. "Think about adaptation. What does a plant need to survive where the rain bars are nearly zero?"

Kayla looked at the scrub's small, hard leaves, then at the tall bars on her rainforest graph, where plants could drink all year. "Here," she said. "Desert. Jayda wins the lunch spot." She packed the graph away and started up the trail after the others, boots crunching over gravel that had not felt rain in weeks.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: French speakers normally address a server with the formal "vous," not the familiar "tu," which is kept for friends, family and children.
story:
Annabelle spread the paper menu across the kitchen table and straightened her fork one more time. On Saturday, her mother would take her to Chez Margot, the French café two streets over, and Annabelle had promised to order for both of them, in French, all by herself. She had inherited a little French from her grandmother, who used to sing to her in it, but songs would not help her ask for a sandwich and find out what it cost.

Kaysen arrived at four o'clock wearing his father's bow tie, ready to play the waiter. He picked up the notebook and put on a terrible accent. "Bonjour, mademoiselle. What would you like?"

"Je voudrais un croissant," Annabelle said. So far, so good. Then she added the part she had practiced with her little cousin Théo on video calls, the part that felt friendly and warm. "Tu as des sandwiches? Combien ça coûte?"

Kaysen scribbled on his pad. "Croissant, sandwiches, très bien." He brought her a plate of crackers and pretended to pour water from an empty pitcher. Annabelle drilled it again and again until the words came out smooth as a slide.

That evening, her cousin called from Lyon, and Annabelle watched the screen while Théo's mother answered the door for a delivery man. Annabelle heard it clearly: "Vous désirez?" Not tu. Vous. The delivery man got vous, and so did the plumber, and so did the baker. Only Théo and his friends got tu. Annabelle sat back. She had been speaking to imaginary waiters the way she spoke to a six-year-old cousin.

She tested it the next day. Kaysen came over again, and this time Annabelle said, "Vous avez des sandwiches? Combien ça coûte?" Kaysen tilted his head. "You changed it," he said. "What happened to the other one?"

"That one's for friends and family and kids," Annabelle said. "A server is a stranger. It's vous for them. It's not rude, it's how it's done." She felt a small ache about it, though. Tu had felt like Théo's kitchen, warm and familiar. Vous felt like standing up straight in a jacket. She had gained the right word and lost the cozy one, at least for strangers.

On Saturday the sky was gray, but the windows of Chez Margot glowed luminous and gold, like the pension in Lyon where her grandmother used to stay. Inside, Annabelle caught her reflection in the glass, took a breath, and turned to the server. "Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais un croissant et un sandwich, s'il vous plaît. Combien ça coûte?"

The server smiled and answered in quick, flowing French that Annabelle only half caught, and her mother leaned over and whispered, "You're ordering for me too, remember."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
story:
Savannah was supposed to be finishing a science project at her grandmother's kitchen table, but Milania kept going quiet whenever the phone buzzed with messages from their class group chat. Finally Savannah leaned over and read the screen upside down. Someone had posted a photo of Milania from gym class with a caption about hygiene, and half the class had replied with laughing faces.

"Send me that photo," Savannah said, which was not what she had planned to say. Milania looked confused but did it. Savannah set the phone down and picked up her poster about hand washing, the one due Monday. "Okay, I need your opinion. Is my drawing of germs too scary, or just scary enough?" Milania laughed for real, and for ten minutes the kitchen was only markers and arguing about how many legs a cartoon germ should have. The teasing did not come up again that afternoon, and Savannah let herself believe her trick had worked.

It had not. On Monday a boy in their class mimicked Milania in the hallway, pinching his nose and making a whiny voice, and three kids laughed. Savannah stepped between them and said, loudly, "The poster's due fifth period, are you even done yours?" The hallway crowd drifted off. But at lunch the boy sat two tables away, and every time Milania got up to get a tray, he made the pinched-nose face again, quieter, so a teacher would never catch it. Savannah saw the pattern: her interruptions stopped each moment, but the moments kept coming back. Something hidden was keeping it alive, and blocking it one hallway at a time was not touching it.

She tried one more thing. She wrote a note and slid it across the table to Milania: If I tell Mr. Ong about the photo and the hallway stuff, is that okay? Milania read it twice, then wrote back underneath, won't that make me a snitch? Savannah stared at the word. In third grade, snitch had meant running to the teacher to get someone in trouble, and everybody hated the kid who did it. But this was different, and she wanted to be sure she could say why. She wrote: it's not tattling if you're trying to protect someone from harm, not trying to get someone in trouble. Milania read it, folded the note into her pocket, and gave a small nod.

They went together at the end of fifth period. Savannah did most of the talking while Milania stood close enough that their sleeves touched. Mr. Ong asked a few questions, looked at the photo, and said he would handle it. He did not make speeches or pull the boy out in front of everyone; by Wednesday the group chat was quiet and the pinched-nose face had disappeared, which is how Savannah knew it had actually worked.

The cost came on Friday. The boy's friends had decided Savannah was the reason he lost his lunch privileges for two days, and they saved her a seat nowhere, saved her a place in their game nowhere, and turned their shoulders when she passed. She ate lunch with Milania and Violet instead, at the far table by the window, and it was quieter there, and lonelier too, and Milania slid half her cookie across the table without being asked. "Tomorrow we finish the germ poster," Milania said. "Yours still has too many legs."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Most bicycle tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air, so a flat usually means a hole in the tube.
story:
Landon crouched beside his bike at the bus stop, staring at the rear tyre like it had betrayed him on purpose. The bike had thumped and wobbled the whole last block, and now the tyre was flat as a pancake. His first plan had been simple: push the bike to the shop and pay for a whole new tyre. But the shop was closed, his phone was dead, and the bus wouldn't take a bike at this hour.

Sara got off the 4:15 and stopped when she saw him. "You know most bike tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air," she said, dropping her backpack on the bench. "A flat usually just means a hole in the tube. You don't need a whole new tyre."

"Inside?" Landon pressed the flat tyre with his thumb. It was limp, but when he squeezed near the rim he felt something soft and tubelike under the rubber, like a garden hose buried in a doughnut. So the tyre he could see was only the outside part. The thing that actually held the air was hidden. That was weird and kind of great, like finding out a wall had wires carrying voltage behind it, invisible until you looked.

Vihaan rode up on his own bike and skidded to a stop. "Ms. Jean-Louis keeps a repair kit in the community centre, but it's locked till five." He dug in his own bag and pulled out two plastic levers and a hand pump. "These are yours if you want to try."

Landon wondered where the hole could be, since he couldn't see the tube at all. He had an idea: if the tube held the air, he could test it before even taking anything apart. He unscrewed the cap, pressed the valve stem, and listened. A sad little hiss came and went. He pumped some air in, then leaned close and moved his ear around the tyre, section by section, like a doctor with a stethoscope. Near the valve, a faint, rhythmic whisper kept going. "There," he said. "The leak's by the valve somewhere."

He worked a lever under the edge of the tyre, then the second one a hand's width away, and peeled the black rubber back. There it was, pale and sagging, the inner tube itself. He lifted it out and found the puncture, a pinhole by the valve stem. Vihaan handed him a patch, Landon stuck it on, and they worked the tube back inside, tucking the tyre edge over the rim with their thumbs. Pumping took longer than he expected, and he had to stop twice to rest his arms, but the tyre rose round and firm. He pressed it. Hard. Permanent, or close enough to get home.

The streetlights flicked on. "Race you to the corner," Vihaan said, and Landon pushed off, the back wheel humming.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
story:
Ellie had promised her grandmother a handmade get-well card, and she was failing badly. Every time she folded the thick cream-colored card stock, the paper cracked along the crease like dry river mud, leaving a bumpy white scar down the middle. She had tried three times. Three ruined cards lay on the kitchen table like evidence at a crime scene.

"You look like you're plotting something sinister," said Maelys, who had biked over with Cash after school. Cash picked up the cracked cards and held one to the light. "It's like the fold has a disease," he said, and Ellie snatched it back before he could make it worse.

"I can't figure out what's wrong," Ellie said. "Thin paper folds fine. Grandma's thin stationery never cracks." She thought back to last winter, when she had helped Mr. Ito, the neighbor across the fence, repair a cardboard model of a lighthouse for the library display. He had run a dead ballpoint pen along a ruler before bending each wall, and every edge had come out crisp and sharp as a tent seam. She had thought he was just being fussy. Now she wondered if it was the whole secret. Maybe the tool mattered, and the pressure, and the line before the fold. She found a blunt plastic stylus from Grandma's craft drawer, lined a ruler up where the fold belonged, and drew the point firmly down the card once. Then she folded it. The card bent along the scored line, clean and smooth, without a single crack.

"It worked!" Ellie held it up so they could distinguish the good crease from the ruined ones, which really wasn't hard, since the old folds looked like lightning bolts and the new one looked like a book spine. Cash immediately demanded to be taught, scored his own card with a wooden spoon handle, and pressed too hard, tearing a tiny hole through the middle. "A valve," he announced solemnly, holding the card up to his mouth and pretending to blow air through it like a pool toy. "Inflatable greeting cards. I'm going to be rich."

That was when Ellie noticed the date on the calendar by the fridge. Grandma came home from the hospital tomorrow, not next week like she'd thought, which meant the card had to be perfect tonight. They worked until dark, and when Ellie finally lettered the last word, Cash and Maelys leaned over her shoulders to look. The front showed a lighthouse, borrowed from Mr. Ito's design, and inside it read, "You guide everybody home." Ellie scored one last line, folded the card shut, and slid it into an envelope before anything else could go wrong.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
Mackenzie had watched Zackary demolish the competition at every practice swim since September, so when he climbed out of the warm-up lane looking like a deflated pool toy, she knew something was wrong. Tryouts for the school team started in exactly forty minutes. There was no second day, no makeup session, no mercy. Ms. Bondarenko had said it once, in her flat voice, and nobody had dared ask her to repeat it.

"You look terrible," Mackenzie told him.

"Thanks." Zackary rubbed his eyes with the heel of his hand. "Everything's blurry. The wall keeps moving."

The wall was not moving. Mackenzie considered the obvious suspects: too little breakfast, nerves, the chlorine. But he wasn't nervous, she was pretty sure, and he'd eaten half a granola bar. She ran through the last two days like a detective rewinding a security tape. Yesterday at lunch he'd been fine. Last night, though, he'd mentioned something about a new game. He'd mentioned it four times. That was a pattern.

"How late were you up?" she asked.

He shrugged, which was its own kind of answer. "One. Maybe two."

"One in the morning?"

"Two, probably," Judy said, sitting down on his towel. "He was posting scores. I saw them. At one-forty."

Mackenzie did the math right there on the wet concrete, counting on her fingers because her brain was also tired, though not as tired as Zackary's. "Sleep experts say kids our age, six to twelve, need nine to twelve hours a night. Teenagers need eight to ten. You got maybe six." She held up her fingers again to check. "You're three hours short of even the lowest number for a kid, and you're still eleven, so you don't even get the teenager discount yet."

"The teenager discount?"

"Teenagers need less. Eight to ten instead of nine to twelve. It's not a discount, it's a rule."

"So I'm extra doomed."

"You're a percentage of yourself," Mackenzie said. "Like seventy percent Zackary."

He considered this with an acute seriousness, staring at the water as if it might apologize. Then Mackenzie had her idea, and since there was no time to be delicate about it, she just said it. "Warm up slow, then sleep at every break. Every single one. Head on the bench, eyes closed, even if it's ninety seconds. Ninety seconds is better than zero."

Zackary swam his heat looking like a man moving through honey, but between heats he lay on the bench with his jacket over his face, and Judy stood guard. When Ms. Bondarenko called the final group, he pulled the jacket off, and his eyes looked almost human again. He won his lane by half a length, then flopped onto the tiles.

"That was seventy percent Zackary," he announced to the ceiling. "Imagine the full hundred."

"Sleep tonight," Mackenzie said. "All twelve hours of it."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In his 1872 book on emotions, Charles Darwin called blushing 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions'.
story:
Jace got to the park twenty minutes early, which he decided was a mistake, because now he had twenty minutes to think about everything that could go wrong. He sat on the bench by the duck pond and turned his phone over and over in his hands. Last week he had told Kaylie he liked her in a text, and she had written back "me too," and then, after a long pause, "want to hang out at the park saturday?" He had read that message maybe forty times. Hasan had helped him plan it, and their plan had exactly one rule: don't try to be someone you're not. Jace was already breaking that rule, because he had worn a shirt he never wore.
