When Kaylie showed up, she had a book under her arm, which was odd for a walk in the park. "Hi," she said, and her face went pink, then red, then redder. "Okay, great, my face is doing a whole thing right now."

"That's fine," Jace said. "Mine was doing it all morning."

"No, but listen to this." She held up the book, which turned out to be about scientists, not a novel at all. "I had to give a presentation yesterday and I picked blushing, because obviously. And I found this guy. In his 1872 book on emotions, Charles Darwin called blushing 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions.'"

"That's the whole quote?"

"That's the whole quote. He actually used those words." She grinned even while her face stayed red. "So basically no other animal does this. It's just us. I've been deciding whether that's embarrassing or the best thing ever."

Jace thought about that while they walked toward the snack stand. If blushing was the most human of all expressions, then hiding it was sort of hiding being human. He tested the idea out loud. "Okay, so here's my theory. If I just confess when I'm nervous instead of pretending I'm not, it should be, like, the least embarrassing option. Scientifically."

"Test it," Kaylie said.

"I'm nervous," he said. "I've been nervous since Tuesday. I practiced saying hi in the mirror."

Kaylie laughed so hard she had to stop walking. Then she said, quietly, "I rehearsed my first sentence on the walk over. The book was going to be my backup topic if things got quiet."

They bought nachos and sat near the fountain, where the wind sprayed them lightly and the cashier called them "our two most loyal consumers of liquid cheese." Kaylie wiped her eyes. "Okay, your theory holds up. That was way less embarrassing than the mirror thing."

Jace remembered his shirt, the one that wasn't him at all, and how crucial he'd thought it was this morning. Now it seemed like the opposite: the crucial thing had been the confessing part. He didn't say that out loud, though. Instead he said, "Want to see the ducks? They can't blush, so they're basically judging us."

Kaylie stood and held out the book. "Bring it. In case we run out of words."

"Deal," said Jace, and they walked toward the pond.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
"You're hyperventilating," Noemie said. "Breathe slower. Regulate it, like Coach says, in through the nose."

Ariah gripped the edge of the lab table and stared at the clock. "Friday, fourth period, the nurse takes it off. You've heard that saw. It screams. I'm not lying, it's a scream." She held up her arm, the white fiberglass ending just past her wrist. "My cousin said it burned all the way through."

"That's not how it works," Noemie said. She shifted her own cast, heavy on her left forearm, six weeks and four days old. The clinic had given her the removal date too, one week behind Ariah's, and she had spent more than one night imagining that sound against her skin.

"You don't know that."

"Actually I do. Watch." Noemie pulled a ruler out of her binder, laid it flat on the table with four inches hanging over the edge, and pressed her palm down on the rest. She flicked the free end. It buzzed, a low angry note. Then she took Ariah's good hand and pressed the vibrating tip against Ariah's fingers. It drummed against them, fast little taps, and stopped. "It's going back and forth, fast. Back and forth, not around. It never spins. That's why it chews through the cast and not you. Hard stuff, it cuts. Skin, it just bounces off."

Ariah pulled her hand back and eyed the ruler. "That's a ruler."

"The nurse did it to me with the actual saw. First visit, because I went white as the ceiling. She ran the blade right across my palm." Noemie held up her right hand, unmarked. "Nothing. Then she touched it to the old plaster and it ate straight through like the plaster was porous paper."

Mr. Chukwu looked up from his attendance sheet. "Rulers are for measuring, Ms. Noemie."

"Demonstrating," she said. "Physics."

"Then demonstrate quietly." He went back to his list, but the corner of his mouth had moved.

Ariah sat down slowly. She picked up the ruler herself, pressed her thumb on it, flicked the end, and held her fingertip against the buzz. Taps, taps, taps, then stillness. She did it twice more. "Back and forth," she said. "Not around."

"Not around," Noemie said.

Ariah put the ruler down and flexed her fingers. Then she took out her phone and typed a note. Friday, 1:15. Bring something to bite. And, in smaller letters underneath, Don't scream, don't scream, don't scream. She turned the screen so Noemie could read it.

"That's a plan," Noemie said.

Ariah snapped the phone shut, stood, and carried the ruler to Mr. Chukwu's desk. "Can we keep this one in the room? I'm going to need it Thursday night, and I'd rather not explain to my mother."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Natalie climbed onto the school bus and slid into the seat behind Grace, who was holding her phone so the screen faced the window. "Look at this," Grace whispered, tilting it back. It was a screenshot of a private chat between Heath and some kid from another homeroom, and every line was about Grace. Heath had called her a drama queen and said she "always has to run everything." The screenshot had landed in a group chat full of kids Grace barely knew.

"He sent that privately," Grace said. "To one person. How does everyone have it?"

Natalie stared at the gray border around the messages, the little time stamp, the name at the top. Somebody had taken a picture of their own screen and passed it around, that much was obvious. What she couldn't see was who. She tried to diagnose the problem like Mr. Mensah taught them in science: start with what you know, then test one thing. She knew the screenshot existed. She knew it was shared. The unknown was the route it traveled.

"Who's in that group chat?" she asked.

"Like fifteen people," Grace said. "It showed up this morning from a girl I've never even talked to."

That was the clue. If the message had stayed between Heath and his one friend, only two people could have shared it. Once it hit a group, though, it belonged to everyone, and any one of them could screenshot it again and send it somewhere new. A private message, Natalie realized, was only as private as the person reading it. Heath had typed it for one friend, and now the whole seventh grade was reading it over breakfast.

"Here's my test," Natalie said, pulling out her own phone. "I'll message the girl who posted it and ask where she got it. If she says a friend sent it to her, we follow it back." She typed, sent it, and watched the dots bounce while the bus rattled over the railroad tracks. The answer came fast: somebody had forwarded it to her from the group chat itself, which meant the screenshot had been circulating even before Grace saw it. Tracing it back to the first person would be like tracing a rumor at lunch. Impossible.

"It doesn't even matter who leaked it anymore," Grace said, slumping against the window. "It's everywhere."

Mr. Mensah got on at the next stop, and Natalie watched him nod good morning without knowing anything about it. On the seat across the aisle, Heath was laughing with his friends, phone out, completely cheerful. Then Grace sat up straight and did something radical. She opened a chat with Heath, typed "I saw what you wrote about me. We should talk," and handed the phone to Natalie. "Screenshot that before I send it," she said. "If he forwards it to make fun of me, I want proof of exactly what I said, word for word."

Natalie pressed the buttons and smiled. "So the trick isn't never writing anything private. It's keeping your own receipt."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Simon had been saving for weeks to buy the blue scarf at the international festival's craft table, because the school store where he usually bought gifts had closed during the recession and his mother's hours at the clinic had been cut. The festival filled the gym with the smell of fried plantains and cardamom, and his job was to guide the younger kids from the elementary wing through the displays without letting anyone wander off.

At the first booth, Anayah was showing a group how people greet each other in Ghana. She pressed her palms together and gave a small bow, then shook hands with a quick snap of the fingers at the end. The little kids tried it, snapping too early and collapsing into giggles. "The snap takes practice," Anayah said, and demonstrated again, slower this time.

Simon noticed that each table had its own pattern. At the Japanese booth, Annabelle wrapped a gift in cloth, folding the corners with sharp creases, and told the kids that the wrapping was as important as what was inside. At the long dinner table set up by the French club, the students kept their hands above the table and tore bread instead of cutting it. Simon began to perceive a rule underneath everything: what counted as polite wasn't random, it was something each place had decided, and the decisions were different everywhere.

He tested his idea at the Thai booth, where a boy named Tan was stacking wooden elephants. A kindergartner with a lopsided ponytail reached up to pet one of the elephants, and Mr. Delacroix, the art teacher, smiled and moved his hand toward her hair to ruffle it in a friendly way. Simon stepped between them before he knew he was doing it. "Wait," he said.

Tan looked up. "In Thailand the head is sacred," he said simply. "Touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be seen as rude."

Mr. Delacroix pulled his hand back and thanked her instead, and the little girl grinned and went back to the elephants. Simon felt his ears go warm. He had guessed right, but only because he had been watching for patterns all morning instead of just looking at the food.

Later, at the craft table, he counted his money and found he was two dollars short of the scarf. He was still doing the math when the kindergartner appeared beside him, dragging a strip of ribbon. "You stopped the head thing," she said. "Tan told me." She held out a paper flower she had folded at the Japanese booth, creases crooked but careful, and Simon remembered Annabelle's demonstration. He received it with both hands and a small bow.

The cashier, watching, knocked two dollars off the scarf. "Festival price," she said.

Simon wrapped the scarf in the ribbon the girl had left behind, folding the corners the way Annabelle had, sharp and slow. Then he handed it back to his mother at the door, palms flat, and bowed exactly as Anayah had taught him.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Benjamin sat at the kitchen table trying to butter toast with his left hand, which was harder than it looked. His right arm, wrapped in its white cast, rested on the table like a useless piece of sports equipment. The cast had been signed by half his class already, and Imane had drawn a dragon on it that curled from his wrist to his elbow.

His little sister slid into the chair across from him, staring at the cast. "Does it hurt a lot?" she asked.

"Only when I bump it," Benjamin said. "Want to hear something weird? The doctor said my arm is only partly broken."

His sister frowned. "How can a bone be partly broken?"

Benjamin picked up the branch his dad had brought in from the yard, the one he'd been carrying around since the hospital visit. He had asked for it on purpose, because he needed to see the thing for himself. He bent it slowly across the table. It cracked on one side, and on the other side it just bent, holding its shape like a green twig instead of snapping clean in two.

"That's what happened to my bone," he said. "It's called a greenstick fracture. It cracks on one side and bends on the other. The doctor says it mostly happens to kids, because our bones are more flexible."

"So you're a green branch," his sister said, and she laughed so hard she nearly fell off her chair.

Later that afternoon, Imane and Kyla came over with a poster board and markers. Ms. Popal, who taught science across the street and had become something of an influential figure in the neighborhood, had offered the class a challenge: explain a medical mystery at the school science night, and the winning team would narrate their demonstration to the whole auditorium.

"A greenstick fracture," Kyla said, writing the words across the top of the poster. "That's our mystery."

"I'll be the adversary," Imane said, grinning. "I'll be the skeptical audience. Convince me."

Benjamin held up the branch and bent it, and Kyla filmed it in slow motion on her phone so the audience could watch one side crack while the other side bowed. They practiced three times, and on the third try the branch snapped clean through, which was not what they wanted at all.

"We need a greener one," Kyla said, and they all trooped out to the backyard to hunt through the pile of trimmings until Imane found a twig that bent exactly right. Benjamin held it up to the light, turned it slowly, and smiled.

"This one," he said. "This one is perfect."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
story:
Harper slid into her seat just as the bell rang, holding the new glasses case like it held a winning lottery ticket. She had waited two weeks for these, two weeks of guessing whether the blur at the back of Ms. Menon's classroom was the whiteboard or just a smudge. Now the case sat on her desk, and she could barely sit still.

"Open it," Deklan whispered from the next row. "Open it right now."

She flipped the case open and the glasses caught the light, thin silver frames with lenses that looked ordinary but weren't, because folded into the receipt tucked underneath was a puzzle. Along the top, next to the right-eye numbers, it said OD. Next to the left-eye numbers, OS. Harper frowned. She had seen those letters at the optometrist's office, and a kid in the waiting room had speculated loudly that they were codes for something serious, maybe a warning the doctors put on file about your eyes. Harper hadn't believed it, but she hadn't known what else they meant either.

"Maybe it's a secret," Deklan said, leaning over. "Like classified."

"Then why would they print it on a receipt anyone can read?" Harper put the glasses on. The whole room snapped into focus, and she actually gasped, because the whiteboard wasn't a smudge at all, it was a list of Latin roots due Friday. She copied it down, then stopped. Right there on the board, third from the bottom: oculus. Eye.

Her hand shot up before she thought it through. "Ms. Menon, does Latin have words for right and left?"

"Try sinister and dexter," Ms. Menon said, and moved on to attendance.

Harper wrote them fast. Dexter, right. Sinister, left. Oculus, eye. She lined them up next to the receipt like a detective matching fingerprints. O-D. Oculus dexter, right eye. O-S, oculus sinister, left eye. "It's the eyes," she said out loud, loud enough that Erica turned around. "OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye. That's all it is. Latin."

Erica leaned in to study the receipt. "So the kid in the waiting room who thought it was a scary code was completely wrong?"

"Completely and gloriously wrong." Harper grinned. "It's not a warning, it's an empire of old words. Like some Roman emperor's doctor writing prescriptions two thousand years ago."

Deklan pointed at the board. "Then dexter must be where dexterous comes from. Good with your right hand."

By lunch, the three of them were hunting Latin through the whole classroom like nocturnal owls swooping on mice, finding television and aquarium and audio on posters and labels. Harper stuck a folded note to Erica's desk before fifth period: "Your OS lens, left eye, is the one that turns everything sharp. Check the mirror. You'll see which one I mean." At the end of the day, Erica slipped a note back, and Harper opened it under her desk.

"Checked it," it read. "Covered my right eye and then my left. You were right about which was which. Meet me at the board, I found another Latin word."

Harper was already halfway across the room.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
Dylan stood in his grandmother's kitchen with his sleeves pushed up, staring at her recipe box. The box was transparent plastic, cracked at one corner, and inside, the cards were jumbled together so he couldn't tell the biscuit recipes from the ones for soup. She had died eight days ago, and tomorrow was the funeral, and he had decided tonight that he would make her honey bread for the reception, because somebody had to and his mother couldn't stop crying long enough to read a recipe.

The problem was that his hands shook, and his stomach turned at the smell of flour. He hadn't eaten much all week. He'd managed half a piece of toast on Monday and a few bites of rice last night, and every night he lay awake until the ceiling went grey with morning. He pressed his palm against his forehead to assess whether he had a fever, the way his grandmother had taught him, but his skin felt normal. He was so tired, though. Maybe he was getting sick on top of everything. Maybe he had caught something at the hospital, during those last afternoons beside her bed.

The doorbell rang. It was Katia, holding a bag of groceries, and behind her Adonis, who lived three streets over and had come because Katia texted him. "Your mom let me in," Katia said. "She said you were attempting the honey bread." Adonis peered at the counter, where Dylan had spilled sugar in a wide, defeated circle. "How much have you eaten today?" Adonis asked, in the flat voice he used when he already knew the answer.

"A banana," Dylan said. "Some of a banana."

Katia opened the fridge, took out the good cheese his mother saved for company, and cut three slices without asking. "You know this is a thing that happens," she said quietly, handing him a slice. "After my grandpa died, my dad couldn't sleep for like two weeks, and he barely ate. The counsellor at the hospice told us grief gets into the body too, not just the feelings. It makes you tired, it messes with your sleep, it changes your appetite." Dylan chewed slowly. The cheese actually tasted like something. "So I'm not getting sick?" he asked. "You're grieving," Katia said. "It's not a parasite, it's not eating you from inside. It's just grief, and it does this."

Dylan looked at the recipe box again, and this time he pulled a card from the middle without caring which one it was. Honey bread, in his grandmother's loopy handwriting, with a note at the bottom: add the orange zest, everyone forgets the orange zest. Adonis found the grater. Katia cracked the eggs. The dough came together sticky and sweet, and while it rose under a towel on the warm stove, the three of them sat on the floor eating crackers, and Dylan realized he was hungry, actually hungry, for the first time in days.

They would eat better at the reception than he had eaten all week, he thought, and that seemed like something his grandmother would appreciate. When the timer buzzed, he opened the oven, and the smell of honey and orange filled the kitchen the way it used to on Sunday mornings when she was still the one holding the pan.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
story:
Jasmine's phone had been at the repair shop since Tuesday, which meant she was doing her science homework on the loaner laptop behind the counter while Mr. Okafor's nephew fixed a cracked tablet in the back. Ms. Dela Cruz, who owned the shop and let Jasmine sit there after school, had said the laptop was ancient, but the spreadsheet program opened fine, and Jasmine needed a bar chart of her data by tomorrow.

The data was Kelly-Anne's fault. Kelly-Anne had decided their biology project would be about venomous caterpillars, specifically the puss caterpillar, whose larva looks like a small tuft of hair and stings anyone who touches it. They had spent two weekends counting larvae on five different trees, and Jasmine had typed the numbers into the spreadsheet: twelve, nine, fifteen, six, eleven, one column of trees and one column of counts. She had the numbers. What she did not have was a chart, because she could not figure out how to make the program add the column.

She called Kelly-Anne, who had the same program at home. "Click on the empty box under your last number," Kelly-Anne said. "The one right below your eleven. Then type the equals sign and the word SUM, and after that, in parentheses, the first cell, a colon, the last cell."

"What's the first cell called?" Jasmine asked.

Kelly-Anne paused, the sound of someone squinting at a screen. "Row 4, column... hold on. It's 4C."

Jasmine typed 4C. The box turned red and a message complained about an error. "It hates me," she said.

"It can't be wrong, it's just a box," Kelly-Anne said. "Try C4."

Jasmine deleted 4C and typed C4, then C5 through C8 after the colon, and hit enter. The total appeared: fifty-three. She sat back. So the box names went letter first, then number. She tried an experiment to be sure, clicking a box in the fourth row and watching the program display its address, D4, letter first again. It was like street addresses, street before the number.

"The chart button is up top," Kelly-Anne said. "Pick the one that looks like bars."

Jasmine selected her two columns, found the button, and clicked. Grey bars sprouted across the screen, the oak tree's fifteen towering over the maple's six. She leaned closer. From the counter, Ms. Dela Cruz glanced over and said, "That's more chart than my whole bank has ever shown me."

"I have to transport this laptop to school somehow," Jasmine said, looking at the screen. "Kelly-Anne, does your bus pass still work?"

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
The bus rattled over the pothole by the gymnasiu, and Henry's phone nearly flew out of his hands. He caught it against his knee and went back to staring at the class group chat, where the argument had already reached forty messages. Someone had posted a photo of Adelle sneezing during the assembly, captioned with three crying-laughing faces, and half the grade had piled on.

"Ms. Yoon says if there's one more blowup, she deletes the whole chat before fourth period," said Johnathan, leaning over the seat. "That's like forty minutes from now."

"So we need rules," Henry said. "Real ones. Not just 'be nice,' because nobody follows 'be nice.'"

Adelle twisted around from the seat in front. "There's no such thing as official rules for a chat. It's the internet. It's a jungle."

"That's what I thought," Henry said, typing fast. "But there's a thing called the Netiquette Guidelines. One of the first written guides to online manners. It was published in 1995, as a document called RFC 1855." The bus's heater roared under the seats, smelling like dust and old pennies, while he scrolled. "It's real. Somebody actually sat down and wrote out how you're supposed to act online."

"Netiquette," Johnathan repeated, grinning. "That's the most beautiful terrible word I've ever heard."

"Careful," Adelle said. "Rule one of your fancy guide is probably don't mock people's beautiful terrible words."

Henry skimmed the document, squinting at the small screen as streetlights strobed across the window. There it was: the difference between how you write to one person in private mail and how you post to a whole group. The photo of Adelle sneezing had gone to everyone, which was exactly the kind of thing the old rules said to think about first. Private stuff, the 1995 people seemed to say, belongs in private.

"Okay," he said. "Here's my formula. One, ask before you post a picture of somebody. Two, if you'd only say it to one person, send it to one person, not all ninety-two of us. Three, the word 'toxic' gets you removed, because if you have to call it that, it already is." He pasted it into the chat and hit send before he could revise it into something weaker. His thumbs were shaking slightly, either from the bus or from nerves.

The messages went quiet. Then the replies started rolling in, one by one: fine, fine, whatever, fine. Someone deleted the sneezing photo. Adelle turned around and gave him a thumbs up so big her whole arm waved.

At the fourth-period door, Ms. Yoon was waiting with her tablet. "I've decided to keep the chat," she announced, "on one condition. It's now the official homework reminder chat. Math only, no jokes, and I read every message."

Henry and Johnathan looked at each other in horror.

"Ninety-two people," Johnathan whispered, "and she just made it the least fun place on earth."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled of burnt coffee and pencil shavings. He slid a checkbook across the table and tapped it twice with one finger. "One thousand dollars," he said. "I'll hold it for five years and give you back twelve hundred. That's my offer, William."

William picked up the checkbook and turned it over. Twelve hundred meant two hundred extra, which sounded fine until he remembered the pamphlet from the credit union in his backpack, the one Shaun had grabbed off the rack outside the gym. Shaun had read it aloud in a vigorous voice, waving it like a fan: "Five percent interest, compounded yearly." William had shoved it in his bag and forgotten it.

He found the pamphlet now, smoothed it on the table between the salt shaker and Grandpa's mug. The credit union would pay five percent, compounded once a year. He did not know what that came to after five years, but he could find out. He took a fresh sheet of paper and wrote the numbers down, and Grandpa watched without saying anything, chewing the end of a toothpick.

First William tried simple interest, five dollars per hundred every year, the same five percent each time. Fifty dollars a year, five years, twenty-five hundred. He wrote $1,250.00 and circled it. That already beat Grandpa's twelve hundred. But the word "compounded" had to mean something different, so he called Shaun from the hallway phone, and Shaun yelled the answer over arcade noise in the background: "Compounded means the interest earns interest too. My sister showed me. There's a chart."

"I'll do my own analysis," William said, and hung up. He ran the compounded numbers on paper, line by line, and when he reached the fifth year he sat back. The total came to $1,276.28. He checked it twice, because it was higher than simple interest, and he could infer that the extra $26.28 came from interest stacking on interest. He slid the paper across the table.

Grandpa held it up to the window light. "Twenty-seven sixty-two more than my offer," he said. "Seventy-six twenty-eight more than nothing."

"Seventy-six dollars and twenty-eight cents," William said. "More than seventy-six dollars, actually."

Grandpa laughed and pulled his own pen from his shirt pocket. He crossed out twelve hundred on the checkbook register, and the pen squeaked against the paper. "Fine. Deposit it Monday. But you're walking to the credit union yourself, and it's raining."

William folded the pamphlet into his back pocket and looked out at the wet sidewalk gleaming past the fence. "I'll take the umbrella with the broken rib," he said. "It still opens."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A pinch flat, often called a snakebite, is two small parallel slits made when an under-inflated tyre hits a sharp edge like a kerb.
story:
Jack had fifteen minutes before the bell, and his bike was lying on the grass behind the gym with its rear tyre flat as a pancake. Malcom crouched beside him, holding the tyre levers like they were surgical tools.

"You narrate the steps while I work," Jack said, popping the first lever under the bead of the tyre. "Mr. Clarke-Williams says that's how you remember them."

Malcom grinned and put on a documentary voice. "The mechanic slides the lever around the rim, careful not to pinch the tube, which the viewer will note is the most important part." He had been reading a memoir about a cyclist who crossed an entire mountain range fixing his own punctures, and now he considered himself an expert on all things with wheels.

Jack worked the second lever under and hooked it to a spoke. The tyre loosened, and he pulled the tube out, blowing a little air into it to find the leak. He turned it slowly under the light, listening for the hiss, and there it was. He stopped. The hole wasn't one hole. It was two small slits, perfectly parallel, about as far apart as the marks of a snake's fangs.

"Look at that," he said quietly. "Two cuts, side by side."

Malcom leaned in. "My cousin calls that a snakebite."

Jack sat back on his heels and thought. A nail would make one hole. Glass would make one rough hole. Two neat parallel slits looked like something had squeezed the tube from both sides at once. He rolled the tyre back and pressed it with his thumb. It gave easily, too easily, like a half-empty water balloon. The tyre had been soft all week, and yesterday he had ridden straight over the kerb by the bike rack at speed, feeling the rim thunk against the concrete. He hadn't thought anything of it at the time, but now the pattern fit. The tyre had been under-inflated, the kerb was a sharp edge, and the tube had been caught and cut in two places at once.

"So it's not the kerb's fault, exactly," Jack said, mostly to himself. "It's flat tyres hitting kerbs. I skipped pumping it because I was lazy." He looked up. "I'm going to check pressure every Monday from now on."

Colton came jogging over from the basketball courts, still holding the ball. "You two need help? I'm biased in favor of doing anything but math review." He knelt down and steadied the wheel while Jack threaded the new tube in, and Malcom narrated the rim tucking with great drama, which mostly meant shouting "careful, careful" at nobody.

The pump hissed and the tyre swelled firm. Jack spun the wheel once and watched it run true. He flipped the bike upright, and his hand was already reaching for the pressure gauge when the bell rang through the yard.

"Ride home?" said Malcom.

Jack looked at the gauge, then at the school gate. "Give me one minute first."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A Python for loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without reaching break, which fits 'no divisor found, so the number is prime'.
story:
The old couch in Florent's basement smelled like dust and popcorn, and Nathan had his laptop balanced on a cushion because the coffee table was buried under Jude's robot parts. Jude was wiring a light sensor for a science project, muttering whenever two wires touched. Nathan's own project was on the screen: a program that would ask for a number and print whether it was prime. Florent leaned over his shoulder.

"It works for nine," Nathan said. "But when I put in thirteen, it prints prime six times." He ran it again and the word prime stacked down the screen, one for every number that did not divide thirteen. Jude set down his sensor and came to look.

"You're printing inside the loop," Jude said. "Move it out."

Nathan tried that, but then every number printed prime once, even nine. He pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes. There had to be a way to say "no divisor found, so it's prime," but only once, and only when it was true. Florent flipped through a printed handout from the coding camp Ms. Gallagher ran at the library, the pages still warm from the car ride. "She showed us something Tuesday. Look." He pointed at a sample loop.

Nathan read it twice. The for loop had an else under it, lined up with the for itself, not inside the loop. "That's not the loop's else," he said slowly. "It's after it."

"It runs only if the loop finished without reaching break," Florent said. "That's what she said."

Nathan stared at the page. Inside his loop he had a break, ready to fire the moment a divisor showed up. If the loop made it all the way through and never broke, that meant no divisor had been found. The else would run exactly then. He inhaled, held it, and retyped the whole thing, fingers slightly too fast, one brace landing wrong so he had to fix it before the program would even start.

"Try nine," Jude said, hovering so close his elbow dug into Nathan's shoulder. Nathan typed 9. Not prime, printed once. He typed 13. Prime, printed once. He typed 25, then 97, then 7919, and the answers came back clean, one line each.

"That," Jude said, "is radical."

"Email it to Ms. Gallagher?" Florent asked.

Nathan hit send, and the little paper airplane icon flew across the screen.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
story:
Layla sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office, staring at the poster about hand washing like it might reveal a secret. The air was humid from the radiator, and her throat still felt like she had swallowed a sweater. Two days ago she had been fine. Then came the fever, the chills, and her mom saying, "Maybe we wait until Saturday, when the office isn't so busy."

"Mom," Layla had said from the couch, wrapped in the quilt Grandma made, "I've been counting. The fever started Tuesday night. If we wait until Saturday, that's four days. I read on the clinic website that prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin. So Saturday's too late for the medicine to do its job."

Her mom had paused with a dish towel in her hand. "You read the whole page? Not just the first paragraph?"

"The whole page. There was also a diagram of a virus wearing a crown, which was weird."

Mom had called that same afternoon. Now here they were, Wednesday, one day into the whole business, and Layla was doing quiet math in her head. Tuesday night to Wednesday afternoon was less than a day. Well within the window. She felt a small, strange pride, the kind that came from catching a rule and using it before it slipped away.

In the corner, Madelyn from science class sat with a box of tissues on her lap like a small sad pet. "Don't tell anyone," Madelyn whispered, "but I've had this since Sunday and my dad said we'd 'let it run its course.' Today my mom overruled him."

"Sunday?" Layla counted backward. Sunday to Wednesday was more than two days. She didn't say anything else about it, because the math said itself, and Madelyn's expression said she'd already figured it out too.

"Lesson learned," Madelyn said, and blew her nose like a trumpet. "Next time I'm dragging my dad in by the ear."

The nurse called Layla's name. On the way down the hallway she passed Mr. Hu, her neighbor, who gave her a thumbs up from behind his mask. "Still alive?" his eyes seemed to ask.

In the exam room, the doctor listened to Layla's chest, then said, "Good timing. We can start the antiviral today."

Layla's mom squeezed her hand. "Thank you for the research department," she said.

"Research department charges a fee," Layla croaked. "One bowl of soup. Payment due in full at home."

"Deal," Mom said, and shook her hand on it, right there on the crinkly paper of the exam table.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends.
story:
Aubrey sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with her notebook open to a page titled "The Gold Collar." The story was about a lost dog named Biscuit, and it ended the moment the kids found him behind the school. She had written the dialogue carefully, remembering the rule about starting a new paragraph each time a speaker changed, and she was proud of the line where Duncan shouted, "Biscuit, come here, boy!" Still, something about the ending felt unfinished, and she couldn't say why.

Her grandfather wandered past with a watering can and paused at her shoulder. "Who's Biscuit?" he asked. She explained the plot: the dog escapes, the kids form a search alliance with the eccentric old mailman who knows every yard on the street, and then the rescue. "Goodness," her grandfather said. "What happened to him after they found him? Did he go home in the truck? Did the mailman ever see him again?" He watered the fern and shuffled on before she could answer.

Aubrey stared at her last paragraph. Maybe that was the problem. The story stopped at its biggest moment, but a reader would want more. She flipped through her class notes, past the page where she had copied examples of punctuated dialogue, until she found a handout with a diagram shaped like a hill. At the peak it said climax. On the downhill slope after it, someone had written falling action and resolution, and beside them, in Mr. Xu's handwriting from the day he'd subbed, "consequences, loose ends." So that was it: after the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. She had drawn the hill in October and never once thought about the downhill side.

She tried it out as an experiment, wondering whether it would really change anything. Duncan, she decided, would carry Biscuit home wrapped in his jacket. The mailman would wave from his route the next morning, and Biscuit would bark once, like a hello. The kids would acquire a habit of walking past the mailman's corner every afternoon, just to check.

She read the new ending aloud to the empty kitchen, and the words did feel different, more settled, like a door closing softly instead of swinging open. Just then her grandmother came in with grocery bags and asked what she was grinning at. "I figured out the downhill part," Aubrey said, and slid the notebook across the table so her grandmother could see the hill with its new, crowded slope.
